museum.name: Pablito
museum.tagline: A museum of paintings that were never painted.
museum.premise: Twenty-five painters, each given a studio in the present day and asked to paint what they see. Nothing here is a copy. Every piece is a new motif rendered the way that painter would have seen it, then chosen by a curator who says no far more often than yes.
promptRules: Never name the artist in a prompt. Describe the hand, the light, the palette and the surface instead.
The subject must be something the painter could not have seen in their lifetime.
One piece, one idea. If the subject needs a sentence to explain, it is two pieces.
Render as a museum photograph of a physical painting. No frames, no text, no signatures.

artists.name: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
artists.wallText: Bruegel painted the village as a swarm: a hundred small lives, each busy with its own errand, seen from a hill just high enough to love them all at once. Give him a city in 2026 and he does not zoom in. He climbs higher.
artists.styleBrief: Sixteenth-century Flemish oil painting on panel, a high vantage point looking down over a sprawling crowded scene, dozens of small figures each absorbed in their own activity, earthy greens, ochres and brick reds against a pale winter or summer sky, meticulous detail across the whole picture with no single hero, gentle satire and warmth, matte surface with fine craquelure
artists.subjectRule: Modern gatherings seen from above. Crowds doing what crowds do now.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the panel painting, even diffuse gallery lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: The Festival
pieces.subject: a vast music festival field at golden hour seen from a hillside, thousands of tiny figures around tents, food stalls, a distant stage with light towers, people dancing, sleeping, queuing for portable toilets, carrying flags
pieces.label: Start at the bottom left, where two couples have given up on the music and lie in the grass in the evening sun. Then climb: striped tents, a row of blue portable toilets with its own queue, flags, and a stage so far off it is a rumour. Bruegel liked a festival best from the hill above it, where you can see every small drama and hear none of the band.

pieces.title: Saturday at the Furniture Store
pieces.subject: a cavernous flat-pack furniture warehouse seen from a mezzanine, hundreds of small figures pushing trolleys through a winding path of room displays, children lost, couples arguing over a sofa, a meatball canteen in the corner
pieces.label: The warehouse is laid out like a village: rooms without ceilings, a bedroom here, a sofa there, and a path that will not let you leave. Children run ahead, trolleys stall, a couple stands in a showroom deciding something about their marriage. Through the far window the real town sits by its river, ignored. Bruegel painted proverbs as places. This one is about going in for a lamp.

pieces.title: Security Line
pieces.subject: an airport security hall seen from a high balcony, a snaking queue of hundreds of travelers with rolling suitcases, removing belts and shoes, trays sliding, a child sitting on the floor, harsh skylight overhead
pieces.label: The queue folds back on itself across the hall, and every loop holds a different small indignity: a belt coming off, a shoe in each hand, a tray sliding into the scanner. A child in red has sat down on the floor, which is the only sensible response. Bruegel never painted a crowd without a child doing exactly this. The spire outside the glass waits for all of them.

pieces.title: The Beginner Slope
pieces.subject: a busy ski resort beginner slope from above, dozens of small figures falling, snowploughing, queuing for a chairlift, a snowboarder sitting in the middle of the run, a café terrace with hot chocolate
pieces.label: The chairlift runs up the middle like a spine, and everything else is gravity. Skiers fall in every direction, a snowboarder sits in the middle of the run as if it were a sofa, and at the left the café terrace is fuller than the slope. In Bruegel's *Hunters in the Snow* the valley below is full of skaters doing much the same. Winter has always been mostly falling over in company.

pieces.title: City Marathon
pieces.subject: a marathon route crossing a bridge seen from a high building, a river of thousands of small runners, spectators with signs, a water station, a runner walking, drones overhead
pieces.label: A river of runners pours across the stone bridge into town, while the real river carries boatloads of spectators underneath. Tables of water cups line the right-hand side. One runner at the bottom has stopped, bent double, and nobody minds. Drones hang over the cathedral where Bruegel would have put crows. He painted whole villages doing one thing at once. This is the same village, in trainers.

artists.name: Caravaggio
artists.wallText: Caravaggio lit his saints with one hard shaft of light from the upper left and let the rest of the world go black. The modern world has replaced that shaft with a phone held at chest height. He would have noticed immediately.
artists.styleBrief: Italian Baroque oil painting, extreme chiaroscuro with a single hard light source cutting figures out of near-total darkness, life-size figures pressed close to the picture plane, dirty feet and real faces, deep blacks, warm flesh tones, blood red and dull gold, dramatic diagonal composition, thick glossy oil surface
artists.subjectRule: Ordinary people caught in one hard modern light: phone glow, fridge light, headlights, a laptop.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, dramatic but even gallery lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: The Calling of the Night Eater
pieces.subject: a man in a t-shirt lit only by an open refrigerator at night, face illuminated from below, reaching for leftovers, kitchen in total darkness behind him
pieces.label: The only light in the kitchen comes from the open fridge, and it lands exactly where Caravaggio's light always lands: the forehead, the forearm, the bare foot. He holds a plastic tub of leftovers like a lamp. The rest of the flat has gone black. Caravaggio painted saints at the moment they were called. This man has been called too. It is two in the morning and the call says eat.

pieces.title: Doubting
pieces.subject: a young woman in bed lit only by the phone she holds above her face, expression of disbelief, sheets and pillows dissolving into darkness
pieces.label: Her phone is the lamp, and the lamp is pointed at her face, where something she has just read has opened her mouth. The sheet is red, the pillows are dissolving, and one bare foot is pushed at us so close you could count the creases. Caravaggio put dirty feet at the front of his altarpieces and was told off for it. Thomas needed a finger in the wound. She needs a second source.

pieces.title: The Supper at the Garage
pieces.subject: three mechanics sharing takeaway food on the hood of a car under a single bare work lamp, one gesturing mid-argument, the workshop black behind them
pieces.label: Three men, a bare bulb on a wire, and a car bonnet for a table, with the foil from the takeaway spread open on the steel. The one in red overalls is mid-argument, hand flung out; the other two are not convinced. Caravaggio's *Supper at Emmaus* has the same flung hand over the same bread, and the same moment of not quite believing it. Their feet are bare, which on a garage floor is devotion.

pieces.title: The Incredulity
pieces.subject: a group of surgeons in scrubs leaning over an operating table lit only by the surgical lamp, one pulling down a mask to look, dark theatre around them
pieces.label: A round lamp overhead, four heads bowed under it, and one surgeon who has pulled his mask down to see for himself. That is the whole story. In Caravaggio's *Incredulity of Saint Thomas*, three men crowd in to watch a finger go into a wound. Here the wound is real and looking is the job. A bare foot sticks out of the dark at the bottom, because some habits of a painter do not wash off.

pieces.title: Judith at the Cash Machine
pieces.subject: a woman in an evening coat at a street cash machine at night, lit hard by the screen and one streetlight, glancing sharply over her shoulder, wet black street behind
pieces.label: Her card is in the machine and her head has snapped round over her shoulder, towards whatever made that sound in the wet street. The screen lights one side of her face, a streetlamp the other. Caravaggio painted Judith in the middle of the deed, frowning as if at a chore. This one has not done anything yet. The figure far down the street should probably take another route.

artists.name: Johannes Vermeer
artists.wallText: Vermeer painted the same room for twenty years: a window on the left, a woman doing something small and absorbing, light that seems to have weight. He would still want the window. He would only want to know what she is looking at now.
artists.styleBrief: Seventeenth-century Dutch interior oil painting, a single figure absorbed in a quiet task beside a window on the left, cool daylight modelling every surface, ultramarine and lead-tin yellow against grey walls, pearly highlights, a tiled floor in perspective, hushed stillness, extremely fine smooth finish
artists.subjectRule: One person, one window, one modern absorption.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, soft even gallery lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Woman on a Video Call
pieces.subject: a woman in a blue cardigan seated at a small table by a leaded window, laptop open, listening on a call, one hand at her chin, a map on the wall behind
pieces.label: She is listening, not talking: chin on her hand, a white earphone wire running down to the laptop, the call going on somewhere far from this room. A map hangs on the wall behind her, as it does in half of Vermeer's rooms. He liked to hang the whole world behind a woman giving her attention to a single letter. The letter now talks back, and the meeting could have been one.

pieces.title: The Baker
pieces.subject: a young man in an apron by a window, scoring a loaf of sourdough with a razor, flour on the table, a jug of water, a pearl earring catching the light
pieces.label: A young man in a blue cap and a yellow apron scores a round loaf with a razor, and the flour on the table has been painted grain by grain. A blue and white jug waits at his elbow. There is a pearl in his ear. Vermeer's *Milkmaid* has poured the same thin stream of milk for three and a half centuries without spilling it. This is the same absorption. The bread also takes three days.

pieces.title: Girl with Headphones
pieces.subject: a young woman glancing back over her shoulder toward the viewer, large white over-ear headphones over a mustard-yellow knitted beanie, a grey plaster wall lit from a window at the left, a phone in her hand
pieces.label: She turns her head at the sound of us, which means the headphones are either off or not very good. The beanie is mustard, the jacket ultramarine, the phone in her hand dark. Vermeer's *Girl with a Pearl Earring* turns in exactly this way, as if someone had just said her name. Nobody knows who she was. Nobody here knows what this one is listening to, and she is not going to say.

pieces.title: The Houseplants
pieces.subject: a woman watering a windowsill of monstera and fern with a brass can, morning light through the leaves, a yoga mat rolled against the wall
pieces.label: Morning comes through the leaded window and straight through the leaves of a monstera, which is the houseplant equivalent of a Delft tile. She tips a brass can with the care Vermeer's women give to a jug or a pair of scales, and a rolled yoga mat leans against the wall like a stick of blue chalk. Nothing happens in this picture. It happens beautifully, and at exactly the right speed.

pieces.title: The Sneaker Repairer
pieces.subject: a man at a workbench by the window cleaning a white sneaker with a small brush, tools laid in order, a stack of shoe boxes, a phone face-down
pieces.label: He is cleaning a white sneaker with a small brush, and he is doing it the way Vermeer's *Lacemaker* makes lace: head down, hands close, nothing else in the world. His tools lie along the bench in the order he will need them. Blue shoe boxes wait on the sill. His phone lies face down beside him, which in 2026 is the most Dutch Golden Age thing a man can do.

artists.name: Francisco Goya
artists.medium: Oil on plaster, transferred to canvas
artists.wallText: Goya painted the last room of his life directly onto its walls, in the dark, for nobody. He had seen a war and a court and a crowd, and he trusted none of them. He would have recognised the comment section at once. He would not have looked away from it.
artists.styleBrief: Late Spanish Romantic oil painting from the black-paintings period, near-monochrome browns, blacks and dirty whites with one passage of blood red, figures with gaping mouths and wide eyes emerging from darkness, coarse dragged brushwork and palette-knife smears, unstable composition, grotesque satire and pity in equal measure, muddy matte surface with cracks
artists.subjectRule: Crowds, fear and appetite in the age of the feed. What people do together when they think nobody is watching, and everybody is.
artists.renderSuffix: flat frontal reproduction of the painting, the canvas fills the frame edge to edge, even lighting, no frame, no wall, no text

pieces.title: The Pilgrimage to the Livestream
pieces.subject: a dense crowd of gaunt faces at night lit only from below by the glow of the phones they hold, mouths open in song or shouting, pressing toward something out of frame
pieces.label: Faces, dozens of them, pressed together in the dark and lit from below by the phones they hold up, mouths open in song or in shouting; it is hard to say which. A woman in a red shawl is caught in the middle of it. Goya painted a pilgrimage on the wall of his house as a march of the singing damned. Whatever they are all singing at is out of frame. It usually is.

pieces.title: Saturn Checks His Phone
pieces.subject: a huge wild-eyed old man crouched in blackness devouring not a body but the bright rectangle of a phone screen, its light on his teeth, his other hand clawed
pieces.label: In Goya's picture Saturn eats his son. Here the old man crams a glowing phone into his mouth instead, eyes starting out of his head, the light on his teeth, his other hand clawing at nothing. Behind him the faces of the crowd scream in the dark. Goya painted the original on the wall of his dining room, which says something about his appetite. This one would look very natural above a bed.

pieces.title: Two Men Arguing in the Replies
pieces.subject: two men sunk to the knees in mud swinging cudgels at each other, each staring not at the other but at a small screen held in the free hand, a flat grey horizon
pieces.label: Two men up to their knees in mud swing cudgels at each other, and neither of them looks. Each is reading the small screen in his free hand, presumably to find out what the other one said. Goya painted the original fight in the same brown field under the same flat sky, and the point was the same: they are sinking, and they will not stop to notice. The reply is loading.

pieces.title: The Group Chat
pieces.subject: a circle of hooded figures leaning together over a single glowing screen in a dark field, faces lit green from below, one of them looking out at the viewer and grinning
pieces.label: A circle of hooded figures leans over one glowing screen in a dark field, and the screen turns their faces green. Most of them gasp. One, at the right, has turned and is grinning, which is worse. Goya's witches gathered round a goat. These gather round a tablet, and the goat is whoever they are talking about. There is always one who looks up to check you saw.

pieces.title: The Dog, Waiting for a Reply
pieces.subject: a small dog's head alone above a vast tilted plane of ochre, looking up at a single blue notification dot floating in an enormous empty brown sky
pieces.label: A great slope of ochre fills the picture, and over its edge a small dog lifts its head towards the sky, where a single blue dot floats. That is all it has. Below, a crowd of faces waits open-mouthed, which Goya did not paint and would have understood. His dog, looking up at nothing, is the loneliest picture in Madrid. This one has a notification. It is not better.

artists.name: Katsushika Hokusai
artists.wing: Thirty-Six Views of Nowhere in Particular
artists.wallText: Hokusai's mountain sat in the corner of almost every print, small and permanent, while the foreground did something reckless. He did not need Mount Fuji. He needed a fixed point and a wave.
artists.styleBrief: Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock print, flat areas of Prussian blue, indigo, ochre and pale cream, bold outlined forms, stylised curling waves and clouds, a small distant landmark anchoring the composition, dramatic foreground movement, visible wood grain and slight registration offset, rice paper texture
artists.subjectRule: A modern fixed point far away, a wave of something in front.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the print on paper, flat even lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the edge of the sheet

pieces.title: Great Wave off the Container Port
pieces.subject: a huge wave seen from the beach, curling from right to left with claw-like foam, a small surfer paddling up its face, a distant container ship with stacked containers small and calm on the horizon, no mountain, a different composition from any famous print
pieces.label: The wave rears up from the right, its crest breaking into claws of foam, and on its face a single surfer paddles for the lip, very small and very keen. Far out on a flat horizon, a container ship sits stacked and indifferent. Hokusai used a mountain as the fixed point in a moving world. The ship will do. It has the same patience, and it is also running late.

pieces.title: Wind Tunnel on the Expressway
pieces.subject: a gust sweeping papers and a plastic bag over an elevated highway, small cars, a wind turbine tiny in the distance
pieces.label: A gust has snatched a plastic bag and a sheaf of papers and thrown them across a raised expressway, where the cars are too small to notice. Far off, beyond the curve of the road, a little snow-capped mountain has turned up after all, next to a wind turbine. In one of Hokusai's prints, travellers on a country road lose a hat and a whole sheaf of papers to the wind. We have kept the papers and added the bag.

pieces.title: Cyclists Crossing at Shibuya
pieces.subject: a wave of cyclists and umbrellas surging across a huge crossing, a single skyscraper tiny and still in the far distance
pieces.label: A wave of cyclists and umbrellas surges across the zebra crossing, so dense that at the left edge it simply turns into a wave, foam and all. In front, a man in a patterned jacket leans into his pedals. Far off, a single thin tower stands still. Hokusai drew crowds the way he drew water, as one mass with a mind of its own. The crossing proves him right every ninety seconds.

pieces.title: Snow at the Charging Station
pieces.subject: heavy stylised snow falling over a row of electric cars at chargers, a figure in a puffer jacket with an umbrella, a distant radio tower
pieces.label: Snow falls in big round flakes, the kind Hokusai carved, over a row of cars asleep at their chargers, each one tethered by its cable. A figure in a puffer jacket walks past under an umbrella, the only thing in the picture that is moving. On the hill a radio tower stands where a temple would be. Hokusai liked weather best when it made people hurry. The cars are in no hurry at all.

pieces.title: Kite Festival with Drones
pieces.subject: dozens of kites and small drones tangled in a stylised gust above a riverbank, tiny figures pulling strings, a distant stadium
pieces.label: Kites fill the sky, a carp, a crest, a hundred diamonds, and among them small black drones have got themselves caught in the strings. On the riverbank, figures lean back and pull. A stadium sits in the distance with a small mountain beyond it. Hokusai drew kites and flying things all his long life with a boy's delight. Nobody has told the drones they are not kites.

artists.name: Caspar David Friedrich
artists.wallText: Friedrich put a person in front of the infinite and turned them to face it, so that we could stand behind them and feel small too. The infinite is still there. The person has a better camera now, and a signal.
artists.styleBrief: German Romantic oil painting, a single figure seen from behind standing before a vast luminous landscape, fog and mist dissolving the middle distance, cold blue-grey and violet dawn light, bare trees and rock rendered with meticulous fine brushwork, immense silence and symmetry, thin smooth glazes, an atmosphere of longing
artists.subjectRule: The sublime, now with reception. Someone alone before something vast that was built or measured rather than grown.
artists.renderSuffix: flat frontal reproduction of the painting, the canvas fills the frame edge to edge, even lighting, no frame, no wall, no text

pieces.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Notifications
pieces.subject: a figure in a dark coat seen from behind, sitting on the low stone wall of a mountain viewpoint beside a coin-operated telescope and an iron railing, holding up a phone to photograph a valley of fog below, the small bright screen the only warm light
pieces.label: He stands with his back to us at the stone wall of a lookout, beside a coin telescope nobody uses any more, and holds his phone up to the valley. Fog fills everything below. The only warm light in the picture is that small screen. Friedrich turned his figures away so that we could look through them into the infinite. This one is looking at the infinite through something else.

pieces.title: Monastery in the Cloud
pieces.subject: a lone figure seen from behind at the edge of a frozen field facing a long low windowless data centre half dissolved in winter fog, a row of bare oaks, a pale sun
pieces.label: A row of bare oaks stands in the fog like mourners, and behind them lies a long low building without a single window. A pale sun hangs over it. On a snowy rock in front, one figure looks across the frozen field. Friedrich's *Abbey in the Oakwood* is a ruin among bare oaks in winter, with monks carrying a coffin towards a church that is no longer there. The monks now work shifts.

pieces.title: Morning at the Wind Farm
pieces.subject: a woman in a long coat seen from behind on a dune at dawn, before a line of enormous white wind turbines fading into sea mist, violet and grey light
pieces.label: A woman in a long coat stands on a dune at dawn, and before her a line of white turbines walks out into the sea mist, each one fainter than the last until they are only a rhythm. The light is violet and grey. Friedrich's women face a sunrise or a sunset they cannot reach, arms open. This one keeps her hands in her pockets. What she is looking at works.

pieces.title: The Airfield in Fog
pieces.subject: a small figure seen from behind at a chain-link fence looking across an empty runway into fog, a distant plane's lights barely visible, the whole scene pale blue and silver
pieces.label: A chain-link fence, a small figure behind it, and beyond them an empty runway running straight into fog, where two lights show that something is coming or going. It is hard to tell which. The whole picture is blue and silver. Friedrich put a monk on a shore before a black sea, so small you have to search for him. Here at least the fence tells you where the edge is.

pieces.title: The Retreat
pieces.subject: two figures seen from behind on a moraine of grey rubble looking at a shrunken glacier far up the valley, a wooden marker post in the foreground, cold clear light
pieces.label: Two figures, one standing with a stick and one sitting on the rubble, look up the valley at a glacier that has shrunk almost out of the picture. A wooden post in the foreground marks where the ice used to be. Friedrich painted *The Sea of Ice* as a wreck of frozen slabs, nature winning outright. Two hundred years later the ice is losing, and people come up at weekends to watch.

artists.name: J. M. W. Turner
artists.wallText: Turner painted the steam engine as if it were a sunset and the sunset as if it were a catastrophe. Every machine of his century dissolved into weather. Ours would too.
artists.styleBrief: English Romantic oil painting, forms dissolving into luminous atmosphere, swirling vortex of golden light, sea spray and storm cloud, a barely legible man-made structure at the centre of the turbulence, impasto scumbled whites and yellows, warm ochre and cold grey, sublime scale, thin glazes and thick highlights
artists.subjectRule: Modern infrastructure swallowed by weather and light.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, even gallery lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Storm, Offshore Wind Farm
pieces.subject: an offshore wind farm in a violent storm, turbines faintly visible through spray and a vortex of cloud, a burst of sun breaking through
pieces.label: A sea like mould, a sky torn into a vortex, and at its centre, barely there, the white cross of one turbine. The sun has broken through at the right and turned the spray to gold. Turner claimed he had himself lashed to a mast to watch a snowstorm at sea. He would have watched this one from the deck of a supply boat, and he would have sent the boat away.

pieces.title: Launch at Dawn
pieces.subject: a rocket launch at dawn, the pad barely visible, the whole sky a column of gold and white vapour reflected in a marsh
pieces.label: The rocket is a white needle at the tip of a column of gold and white vapour, rising out of a marsh so flat and still that it catches the whole launch upside down. The gantry is a grey smudge. Turner painted light that seems to come from behind the canvas. This light comes from underneath, at several thousand degrees, and he would not have wanted to be anywhere else.

pieces.title: Fog, Data Centre, Evening
pieces.subject: a long low data centre building dissolving in fog at sunset, cooling towers steaming, orange light bleeding across wet ground
pieces.label: The sun sets at the left, cooling towers steam at the right, and between them a long low building dissolves in fog across wet, orange ground. You cannot tell weather from exhaust, and Turner would not have tried: in his pictures steam and rain are the same brushstroke. The building is where the cloud lives now, so it is only fair that it should disappear into one.

pieces.title: Rain, Steam and Jet Engines
pieces.subject: an airliner taking off into a rainstorm, blurred runway lights, spray and exhaust heat merging with cloud, a sliver of sun
pieces.label: An airliner lifts off at the left into a funnel of rain and cloud, runway lights smearing beneath it, a control tower caught in the eye of the storm. A sliver of sun burns in the top corner. Turner's *Rain, Steam and Speed* sent a train across a bridge towards the viewer. Nearly two centuries on the machine has left the ground, and the weather is still the faster of the two.

pieces.title: Blizzard on the Motorway
pieces.subject: a motorway in a blizzard, headlights and tail lights dissolving into a white and amber vortex, a bridge barely suggested
pieces.label: Headlights come at us out of a white and amber vortex, tail lights go away from us, and a bridge floats in the middle of the storm as if it were holding nothing up. There are no cars to speak of, only light doing what cars do. Turner painted snowstorms with no horizon at all. This is the motorway at five o'clock on the last Friday before Christmas.

artists.name: Claude Monet
artists.wallText: Monet painted haystacks, a cathedral and a lily pond over and over, because none of them was the subject. The light was. He would find a new pond in five minutes.
artists.styleBrief: French Impressionist oil painting, broken dabs of pure colour, no black, forms suggested by shimmering light rather than line, lavender shadows, pinks and greens vibrating together, reflections on water, plein-air freshness, thick short brushstrokes, canvas weave visible at the edges
artists.subjectRule: A modern surface that catches light: glass, water, screens, wet asphalt. Painted as a series.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, soft even gallery lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Solar Field, Morning Mist
pieces.subject: a field of solar panels in morning mist, panels catching pink and blue light, wildflowers in the foreground
pieces.label: Mist lies on the stream, the sun is a pink coin, and the solar panels step back into the haze like a row of wet slates. The wildflowers in front take all the colour the morning has. Monet painted the same haystacks in every light, and the same poplars along the same river. Solar panels are the haystacks of our fields: they are there to be looked at by the sun.

pieces.title: Solar Field, Noon
pieces.subject: the same field of solar panels at hard noon, glare and violet shadows, heat haze
pieces.label: The same field, six hours later. The mist has gone, the sun is a white blaze overhead, and the panels flash it back so hard the paint turns to glare. The shadows beneath them are violet, as Monet's shadows always were. He would have set up here at dawn and come back at noon with a second canvas. The panels, unlike the haystacks, have been working the whole time.

pieces.title: Rooftop Pool, Evening
pieces.subject: a rooftop swimming pool at dusk reflecting glass towers and a lavender sky, one swimmer, ripples broken into dabs of colour
pieces.label: A rooftop pool at dusk, so full it seems to run off the edge of the building into the city, and every glass tower is broken into dabs on its surface. One swimmer, just a head, cuts through the reflection. Monet spent the last thirty years of his life painting one pond. Give him this one and he would stay, although he would ask them to turn the music off.

pieces.title: The Car Wash
pieces.subject: a car seen through a curtain of soapy water and spinning brushes, colour dissolving in foam and light
pieces.label: A car comes at us head-on through a curtain of soapy water, its headlights two warm smudges, while the brushes spin red and green on either side. The car dissolves into foam, which is what Monet did to the front of Rouen Cathedral: he let the light eat the stone. Here the light has help from a jet wash. Seven minutes, the whole cycle, and a new painting every time.

pieces.title: Glass Station, Rain
pieces.subject: a modern glass railway station roof in rain, commuters as coloured smudges, umbrellas, reflections on the wet platform
pieces.label: Rain on a glass roof, iron columns, a train waiting, and the commuters reduced to coloured strokes under umbrellas: a red one at the front, a blue one further back. The wet floor doubles everything. Monet painted the Gare Saint-Lazare again and again for its steam. There is no steam any more, so he has painted the rain instead, and it does exactly the same job.

artists.name: Vincent van Gogh
artists.wallText: Van Gogh wrote that he wanted to paint the night café as a place where you could ruin yourself. He painted his bedroom, his chair, his postman. The ordinary set on fire. The ordinary has changed. The fire has not.
artists.styleBrief: Post-Impressionist oil painting, thick directional impasto strokes that swirl and vibrate, cobalt and chrome yellow in violent harmony, outlined forms, exaggerated perspective, energetic sky and ground, emotional intensity in ordinary subjects, heavy paint texture casting its own shadows
artists.subjectRule: The small rooms and night places of a modern life, painted with too much feeling.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, even gallery lighting revealing impasto, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: The Night Kiosk
pieces.subject: a 24-hour convenience store at night under an overcast sky with no moon and no stars, harsh yellow interior light swirling out onto blue pavement, one customer inside, a scooter parked outside
pieces.label: There are no stars tonight. The sky has clouded over and all the light in the picture pours out of the shop, where it is always three in the morning. Van Gogh painted the café terrace at Arles from the dark side of the street, as a place to stand outside of. The kiosk puts you in the same spot: one customer at the counter, a scooter left where the cart would have been.

pieces.title: Bedroom in a Shared Flat
pieces.subject: a small bedroom with a mattress on the floor, a laptop on a crate, a string of fairy lights, a bicycle against the wall, tilted perspective
pieces.label: A mattress on the floor under a rumpled blue duvet, a laptop on a milk crate, fairy lights along the ceiling and a bicycle hung on the wall because there is nowhere else to put it. The floor tilts like the deck of a boat. Van Gogh painted *The Bedroom* in Arles three times to show his brother how restful it was. The perspective disagreed with him then. It still does.

pieces.title: Sunflowers in a Water Bottle
pieces.subject: a bunch of sunflowers stuffed into a plastic water bottle on a kitchen counter, yellow on yellow, thick paint
pieces.label: Sunflowers jammed into a plastic water bottle on a yellow counter against a yellow wall: yellow on yellow on yellow, which is how Van Gogh set out to paint his sunflowers, to see whether it could be done. The bottle is the modern part, and he paints it as lovingly as a vase. There is a sink, and a pot of spoons, because this is a kitchen and somebody lives here.

pieces.title: Starry Night over the Ring Road
pieces.subject: a night sky of long horizontal streaks of cobalt and yellow over an elevated ring road with streaming headlights, a tall steel radio mast with red lights in the foreground, no cypress, no spirals, no crescent moon
pieces.label: The sky is laid in long horizontal streaks of cobalt and yellow, a night made of traffic rather than stars. Below it the ring road curves away in ribbons of headlight, and in front a steel radio mast climbs the whole height of the picture, red lights blinking. Van Gogh put a cypress in exactly that place, a dark flame between earth and sky. The mast does the same job, and transmits.

pieces.title: Portrait of the Delivery Rider
pieces.subject: a portrait of a young delivery rider in a bright orange jacket and helmet against a swirling green background, tired direct gaze
pieces.label: A young man in an orange jacket and helmet looks straight at us, tired, patient, not smiling, the insulated bag still on his back. The green behind him swirls. Van Gogh painted the postman Roulin six times, and his whole family besides, because a man who carries things for a living has a face worth the paint. The jacket is loud. The eyes are not.

artists.name: Georges Seurat
artists.wallText: Seurat built pictures out of dots because he believed the eye would do the mixing. It does. Every screen you own works exactly the way he said it would. He died at thirty-one, before anyone could tell him he had been right.
artists.styleBrief: Neo-Impressionist pointillist oil painting, the entire surface built from thousands of small separate dots of pure colour that mix in the eye, complementary pairs of orange and blue and violet and yellow, stiff frieze-like figures in profile, still formal composition, dappled light, a painted dotted border at the edge, matte chalky surface
artists.subjectRule: Leisure in public, held very still. Parks, beaches and queues, seen as if everyone had been asked not to move.
artists.renderSuffix: flat frontal reproduction of the painting, the canvas fills the frame edge to edge, even lighting, no frame, no wall, no text

pieces.title: A Sunday on the Island of Free Wi-Fi
pieces.subject: a riverside park on a Sunday afternoon with stiff figures in profile on the grass, several on e-scooters, one flying a small drone, a woman with a pram and a phone, dappled light
pieces.label: A Sunday by the river, and everyone holds still. Two riders stand on e-scooters, a man in a cap flies a drone over the water, and a woman in a red dress checks her phone with one hand on the pram. Sailboats wait. Seurat spent two years on *A Sunday on La Grande Jatte*, dot by dot. It would take him longer now: everyone keeps turning round to take a picture.

pieces.title: Bathers at the Charging Point
pieces.subject: young men resting on a riverbank in the heat, one charging a phone from a small solar panel, a paddle-boarder on the water, a distant bridge and a factory chimney
pieces.label: Two young men sit on the riverbank in the heat, one hugging his knees, one reading his phone, which is charging from a small solar panel propped in the grass. A paddle-boarder stands on the water. Behind them, a bridge of arches and a factory chimney, still smoking. Seurat's *Bathers at Asnières* had the same chimneys at their backs. The heat has gone up. The chimneys have stayed.

pieces.title: The Queue for the New Phone
pieces.subject: a long line of upright figures in profile waiting outside a glass shop front at dawn, folding chairs, coffee cups, a security guard, pale early light
pieces.label: A line of people stands in profile outside a glass shop at dawn, coffee in hand, folding chairs ready, and at the door one security guard with his cap on. Nobody speaks. Seurat liked his figures as stiff as chess pieces and his light pale and early, and he liked a city that kept still for him. This queue would keep still for anything. It has been here since Thursday.

pieces.title: Circus Sideshow, Livestreamed
pieces.subject: a night crowd seen from behind watching a stage lit by a huge LED screen, their heads a row of dark silhouettes, the screen's light in tiny dots on the backs of their necks
pieces.label: We stand at the back of a crowd at night, looking past a row of heads at a stage where a band plays on a giant screen, and the screen's light falls on the backs of every neck in coloured dots. Seurat painted *Circus Sideshow* by gaslight to find out what artificial light does to colour. The screen is doing exactly what he said it would: building the picture out of dots.

pieces.title: Models, Posing
pieces.subject: three figures at a gym mirror photographing themselves, one from the back, one in profile, one frontal, towels and water bottles, flat even light
pieces.label: One woman, three times: from the back, in profile and from the front, each time holding her phone up to the gym mirror, a towel round her neck, a water bottle in the other hand. Seurat's *Models* is one model in three poses in his studio, with his own big Sunday painting on the wall behind her. The mirror has made the job easier. It has not made it any quicker.

artists.name: Gustav Klimt
artists.medium: Oil and gold leaf on canvas
artists.wallText: Klimt wrapped his sitters in gold until only their faces and hands remained human. The gold was pattern, ornament, armour. Today the armour is different. The faces are the same.
artists.styleBrief: Viennese Secession painting with gold leaf, figures whose faces and hands are rendered softly and realistically while their bodies dissolve into flat fields of ornamental pattern, spirals, squares and eyes in gold, black and jewel tones, mosaic-like decorative surfaces, elongated composition, shimmering metallic leaf against matte paint
artists.subjectRule: Modern intimacy and modern ornament. Tattoos, screens and textiles become the gold.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the painting with gold leaf catching light, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: The Selfie
pieces.subject: two young women standing side by side and upright, cheek to cheek, both facing the viewer and grinning at the phone one holds up, faces soft and real, their bodies and the phone dissolving into a wall of gold ornament and spirals
pieces.label: Two young women pressed cheek to cheek, grinning at the phone one of them holds up, and below their faces everything turns to gold: spirals, eyes, squares, a tree of life curling up the right-hand side. The phone itself is half gilded. Klimt kept the faces soft and real and made everything else into ornament. The selfie does the same. The filter is the gold.

pieces.title: Portrait of a Tattooed Man
pieces.subject: a portrait of a shaven-headed man whose tattoos flow off his arms and become a flat gold and black patterned field around him
pieces.label: He sits square to us, shaven head, level gaze, both arms sleeved in blue-grey tattoos, and at the shoulder the tattoos stop being skin and become the gold field around him: spirals, eyes, black and gold rectangles. Klimt dressed his sitters in pattern until you could not tell the dress from the wall. This sitter has done that himself, over several years and at some expense.

pieces.title: The Embrace on the Platform
pieces.subject: a couple seated shoulder to shoulder on a platform bench, both looking down at one phone, their coats merging into one field of gold rectangles and eyes, a blurred train behind, no embrace
pieces.label: They sit on a platform bench, heads together, both looking down at the one phone he holds, and their two coats have become a single field of gold rectangles, eyes and blossoms. Behind them a blue train blurs past. Klimt's *Kiss* wraps two lovers in one golden cloak. This is the same cloak on the 7.42, and they are not kissing, which is somehow more intimate.

pieces.title: Woman with Controller
pieces.subject: a woman reclining with a game controller, her hoodie and blanket a mosaic of gold and violet squares, her face lit softly
pieces.label: She reclines under a hooded blanket of purple and gold squares, a controller in her hands and her eyes somewhere else entirely. Behind her, pale women in gold drift and doze as in one of Klimt's friezes, as if the game had leaked out of the screen. Klimt painted women at rest as though rest were a jewel. He would have liked the blanket. He would have made it heavier.

pieces.title: The Nurse
pieces.subject: a nurse in scrubs seated after a night shift, face exhausted and tender, her uniform a flat field of gold and teal geometric pattern
pieces.label: A nurse sits at the end of a night shift, head propped on her hand, stethoscope still round her neck, her face tender and wrecked. Her scrubs have become a chequerboard of gold and teal, as though the hospital had issued her an icon's robe. A pale figure watches over her shoulder. Klimt gilded the rich women of Vienna. This is who he should have been gilding.

artists.name: Hilma af Klint
artists.medium: Tempera and oil on paper and canvas
artists.wallText: Af Klint painted diagrams of things she believed she had been told: spirals, petals, letters, the evolution of the soul in pastel. She hid the work for decades. Today's systems are just as invisible and just as ready to be drawn.
artists.styleBrief: Early twentieth-century spiritual abstraction, large diagrammatic compositions of spirals, concentric circles, petals and snail shells in pale pink, egg yellow, sky blue and lilac on a cream ground, delicate line work with small lettering-like marks, symmetrical mystical schemas, tempera flatness with visible pencil underdrawing
artists.subjectRule: Invisible modern systems drawn as spiritual diagrams: networks, algorithms, DNA, the cloud.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the painting on canvas, flat even lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: The Ten Largest, No. 11: Notifications
pieces.subject: a large pastel diagram of a spiral of concentric circles connected by delicate lines, small buds and rings suggesting messages radiating outward, pink and yellow on cream
pieces.label: Rings inside rings, pink, yellow and lilac, and from the centre small buds on fine lines radiate to the edges of the cream ground, where spirals turn in each corner. Af Klint called her biggest canvases *The Ten Largest* and said they showed the ages of a human life. Number eleven shows the ages of a phone, which arrive every few seconds and each want an answer.

pieces.title: Primordial Chaos, Sequenced
pieces.subject: a twisting double spiral of pale blue and pink petals ascending a cream ground, small dots and letters along its length
pieces.label: A rope of pale blue and pink twists up the middle of the picture from a lotus at the bottom to a flower at the top, and it is hard not to read it as a double helix. On either side, flowers and discs repeat like the letters of a code. Af Klint was painting the spiral as the path of life in 1907. Watson and Crick were forty-six years behind her.

pieces.title: Altarpiece for the Cloud
pieces.subject: a triangle of stacked rainbow bands rising to a golden circle, small spirals at the base, symmetrical and serene
pieces.label: A triangle of rainbow bands rises from a pair of spirals at the base to a small golden sun at the top: symmetrical, serene, and a little like the beam of a projector. Af Klint's altarpieces climb in exactly this way, a pyramid of colour ascending towards the divine. The cloud has the same shape in every diagram of it, and roughly the same relationship to belief.

pieces.title: The Swan, Recommended
pieces.subject: two mirrored abstract swan forms in black and white meeting at the centre of a circle divided into coloured segments like a pie chart
pieces.label: Two swans meet beak to beak in the middle of a circle cut into pink, yellow, blue and violet slices, like a pie chart that has taken up religion. A lotus opens above them. Af Klint painted a whole series of swans about opposites finding their way to each other. The algorithm also brings opposites together. It calls the result engagement and keeps them there.

pieces.title: Evolution, No. 9: Charge
pieces.subject: a vertical stack of pastel lozenges connected by thin lines, each holding a small snail spiral, filling from grey at the bottom to gold at the top
pieces.label: A column of lozenges climbs the middle of the picture, each holding a small snail-shell spiral, and they fill from grey at the bottom through pink and blue to gold at the top. It reads as a soul evolving, and as a battery charging. Af Klint's evolution paintings move the soul upwards through colour in exactly this way. She never had to wait at twenty per cent.

artists.name: Edvard Munch
artists.wallText: Munch painted what a feeling does to a room: the sky bends, the floor tilts, the people go pale. He was describing the inside of one head. It turns out to be the inside of everyone's, checked roughly every four minutes.
artists.styleBrief: Norwegian Expressionist painting in thin oil and tempera on rough board, long undulating strokes that bend sky, water and floorboards into waves, sickly blood-orange and deep blue and acid green, one pale mask-like face with hollow eyes and no other faces anywhere, bare cardboard showing through the paint, raw emotional distortion, a sense of dread
artists.subjectRule: The private emergencies of connected life. What waiting, reading and not replying do to a body.
artists.renderSuffix: flat frontal reproduction of the painting, the canvas fills the frame edge to edge, even lighting, no frame, no wall, no text

pieces.title: The Notification
pieces.subject: a figure leaning on the rail of a long wooden bridge at sunset, back half turned to the viewer, holding a phone loosely at their side and staring down at the water, the orange sky and blue fjord bending in waves around them, two dark figures walking away, no hands raised to the face, no open mouth
pieces.label: A figure leans on the rail of a long bridge, head bowed, a phone hanging loose in one hand, and the orange sky and blue fjord swirl around him as if the news had reached the landscape first. Two dark figures walk away at the far end. Munch said he heard a scream pass through nature on a road like this one. Here the scream is silent, and on vibrate.

pieces.title: Typing…
pieces.subject: a young woman alone in a dim room staring down at a phone on the table, three grey dots glowing on its screen, the walls and floor swaying, her shadow huge behind her, bare walls with nothing hanging on them, no window, no other figure
pieces.label: She sits at the table with her hands pressed to her face, staring down at the phone, where three dots glow and glow. The floorboards ripple, the walls sway, and her shadow stands up behind her twice her size. Munch painted jealousy, fear and the sickroom as weather inside a room. He would have known this one at once. It is the longest thirty seconds in the world.

pieces.title: Evening on the Sofa, 4,312 Unread
pieces.subject: a pale man lying alone on a sofa in a green room lit only by a laptop, the screen light on his face, the room lines curving inward toward him, bare walls with nothing hanging on them, no window, no other figure
pieces.label: A pale man lies on a green sofa in a green room, his face lit by the laptop propped on his chest, and every line of the room, walls, ceiling and floor, bends in towards him as if the room itself were leaning in to read. Munch's people are often trapped by the architecture. This one is not trapped. He could get up at any time. He will not.

pieces.title: By the Charging Cable
pieces.subject: a pale girl propped in a chair by a window, a phone charging on the sill beside her, a woman with bowed head at her side, thin scraped paint, dawn light
pieces.label: A pale girl sits propped in a chair by the window, where the sun is coming up red over the water and her phone is charging on the sill. The woman beside her bows her head so low we cannot see her face. Munch painted his dying sister again and again for forty years, scraping the paint back each time. The cable is new to this room. The rest of it is his.

pieces.title: The Dance of Life, Filmed
pieces.subject: couples dancing on a shore at midsummer night under a low moon, one woman in white at the edge filming them on a phone, one in black watching her
pieces.label: Couples turn on the shore under a low moon and its column of light on the water, and at the left a young woman in white stands apart, filming them. At the right a woman in black watches her do it. Munch's *Dance of Life* sets a woman in white and a woman in black at either end of the dance, hope and grief. The one in white has found something to do.

artists.name: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
artists.wallText: Toulouse-Lautrec drew the night from a table at the back, close enough to see the make-up and the tiredness. His posters sold the show and told the truth about it at the same time. The show is still on. It just streams now, and the back table is the one holding the camera.
artists.styleBrief: Belle Époque colour lithograph poster, flat bold areas of red, black, mustard and cream, sinuous confident contour lines drawn in crayon, figures cropped sharply at the edges and seen from low tables, spattered tone, faces caricatured with tenderness and fatigue, large empty areas left as paper, gritty printed texture
artists.subjectRule: Nightlife as work. The performers, the servers and the people who film them, after the glamour has clocked off.
artists.renderSuffix: flat frontal reproduction of the poster on paper, the sheet fills the frame edge to edge, even lighting, no frame, no wall, no lettering, no text

pieces.title: At the Club, Ring Light
pieces.subject: a young woman in a black dress leaning toward a phone on a small tripod with a ring light, her face lit flat white, dancers as a dark blur behind her, a bored barman
pieces.label: She leans towards a phone on a little tripod, her face flattened white by a ring light, lips pushed into a pout that is entirely for the lens. Behind her the dancers are red and black blurs, and the barman rests his chin on his hand, bored beyond boredom. Lautrec loved the performers and never pretended it was not work. Neither does the barman. He sees this show every night.

pieces.title: The DJ
pieces.subject: a DJ in profile behind a booth of laptops, headphones half on, lit green from the screens, a mass of raised phone screens in the crowd below cropped at the bottom edge
pieces.label: The DJ leans over his laptops, headphones on one ear, face turned green by the screens, and below him the crowd has raised a small forest of phones, the faces jammed against the bottom of the picture with their eyes shut. Lautrec cut his figures off at the edge of a poster the way a camera cuts them now. He would have drawn the phones. He would not have raised one.

pieces.title: The Rider's Break
pieces.subject: a food delivery rider slumped on a café chair at one in the morning, helmet on the table, insulated bag at his feet, scrolling his phone under a red awning
pieces.label: A delivery rider in a red jacket slumps on a café chair at one in the morning, chin in one hand, phone in the other, his helmet on the little round table like a second head. The bag waits at his feet, red on red. Behind him, a streetlamp and pale Paris façades. Lautrec drew the people who worked the night while others enjoyed it. The rider is working. This is his break.

pieces.title: Backstage, Between Sets
pieces.subject: a drag performer at a dressing-room mirror ringed with bulbs, half in make-up, checking a phone with one hand and fixing a lash with the other, a tired stagehand behind
pieces.label: She sits at the mirror in a feather boa and a great red wig, half her face made up, fixing a false eyelash with one hand and checking her phone with the other. Behind her a stagehand with a towel on his shoulder looks as tired as a man can look. Lautrec drew performers backstage more often than on it. The eyelash is the show. The phone is the reviews.

pieces.title: Karaoke, Tuesday
pieces.subject: a middle-aged man singing at a karaoke machine in an almost empty bar, two friends filming him with phones, a waitress carrying glasses past cropped at the edge
pieces.label: A middle-aged man in a loosened red tie sings into the microphone with his eyes shut, meaning every word. Two friends in the foreground film him, and their screens show him back to us, small and red. A waitress with a tray of glasses is cut off by the top edge. Lautrec loved an entertainer who was not quite good enough. He would have made this man a poster.

artists.name: Wassily Kandinsky
artists.wallText: Kandinsky heard colour. He painted music as circles, wedges and lines and gave the canvases numbers instead of names. There is more sound now. He would need bigger canvases.
artists.styleBrief: Early twentieth-century abstract oil painting, floating circles, wedges, arcs and thin black lines in a dynamic composition, primary reds, yellows and blues against pale grounds, geometric forms in tension with free painterly marks, musical rhythm and movement, matte oil surface
artists.subjectRule: Modern sounds and signals as pure abstraction. Each piece is a specific noise.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, flat even lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Composition: Notification
pieces.subject: an abstract composition of a sharp yellow triangle striking a large calm blue circle, small black lines scattering outward like a startled sound
pieces.label: A sharp yellow wedge drives into a big calm blue circle, and a spray of short black lines bursts from the point of impact like a startled sound. Everything else, a red sun, a black moon, small triangles, holds its breath. Kandinsky heard yellow as a trumpet and deep blue as an organ. This is the trumpet interrupting the organ at dinner, face up on the table.

pieces.title: Improvisation: Club, 4 a.m.
pieces.subject: a dense abstract composition of repeating dark circles in a rising grid, pierced by red and magenta diagonals and a burst of white
pieces.label: Rows of dark circles climb in a steep grid from the bottom left, growing as they rise, and two diagonals of red and magenta slice through them towards a white explosion at the right. It is loud. Kandinsky painted his improvisations as quick answers to music he had heard. This one answers a kick drum at a hundred and thirty beats a minute, in a room without windows, at four.

pieces.title: Composition: Held Call
pieces.subject: an abstract composition of a single long thin horizontal line across a pale grey ground with small evenly spaced circles in muted colours
pieces.label: One thin horizontal line crosses the grey ground from edge to edge, strung with small coloured dots at even intervals, while a red sun, a blue moon and a few wedges and arcs drift around it without touching it. It is the line you hear while you wait. Kandinsky gave his paintings the names of music. This one is a single held note, with the hold music orbiting it.

pieces.title: Composition: Stadium Roar
pieces.subject: an abstract composition of a huge orange arc rising from a mass of small overlapping coloured semicircles, black wedges pointing inward
pieces.label: A huge orange arc sweeps up out of a heap of small overlapping semicircles, red, yellow, blue and black, while black wedges drive in from the edges. The heap is the crowd. The arc is the noise it makes when the ball goes in. Kandinsky thought a painting could sound like a symphony. This one sounds like sixty thousand people who have all just stood up at once.

pieces.title: Improvisation: Electric Motor
pieces.subject: an abstract composition of nested circles in cool blues and greens with a faint smooth spiral, one tiny red dot, almost silent
pieces.label: Rings of blue and green nest inside one another at the top left, a faint spiral unwinds beside them, and at their centre sits one tiny red dot. That is the motor. Around it the rest of the picture keeps busy, triangles and circles going about their business, but the rings hardly seem to turn. Kandinsky loved a machine. This one would have puzzled him: all that power, and no sound.

artists.name: Henri Matisse
artists.wallText: Late in life, too ill to stand at an easel, Matisse cut painted paper with scissors and pinned it to the walls. He called it drawing with scissors. The joy in those rooms is portable. It fits any apartment.
artists.styleBrief: Mid-century paper cut-out composition, bold flat shapes of saturated gouache-painted paper in blue, coral, green and yellow pinned on a white ground, organic leaf and figure silhouettes, joyful simplicity, visible cut edges and pin marks, decorative rhythm, no shading
artists.subjectRule: Modern domestic joy as flat cut paper: balconies, plants, swimming, dancing at home.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the cut-paper work on white, flat even lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: The Balcony Garden
pieces.subject: a small balcony crowded with potted plants in bold cut-paper shapes, a folding chair, a laundry line, blue sky, coral railing
pieces.label: A balcony in cut paper: pots of monstera and lemon, a striped deckchair, a coral railing, a washing line of towels and shirts against the blue, and a blue cat sitting at the bottom as if it owned the place, which it does. Pins still show where the shapes were fixed. Matisse spent his last years making gardens he could no longer walk in. This one is a metre deep.

pieces.title: The Public Pool
pieces.subject: blue cut-paper swimmers in various poses on a white ground with a band of turquoise water and orange floats
pieces.label: Blue swimmers dive, float and bob through a band of turquoise water, a woman lies on an orange lilo, someone sits in a rubber ring, and orange balls hang in the air as if thrown a moment ago. A yellow sun and fronds of weed fill the white. When he could no longer get to the sea, Matisse cut a swimming pool out of paper and ran it round the walls of his dining room.

pieces.title: Dancing in the Kitchen
pieces.subject: two simplified figures in cut coral and blue paper dancing in a kitchen indicated by a green table and a yellow lamp
pieces.label: Two figures, one coral and one blue, dance in a kitchen that exists only as a green table, a green chair, a bowl of salad and a yellow lamp. Their arms go up. The leaves go up with them. Matisse painted *Dance* as five red figures in a ring on a hill. Here it has come indoors, gone down to two, and is on its second glass.

pieces.title: Monstera and Speaker
pieces.subject: large cut-paper monstera leaves in three greens beside a small black cylinder speaker on a white ground
pieces.label: Big monstera leaves in three greens crowd the top of the sheet, and at the bottom a small black cylinder speaker sits beside a blue seated figure with a hand to her head, listening, or waiting for it to hear her. A little yellow dancer skips at the left. Matisse's cut-outs are full of leaves and blue nudes. The speaker is the only thing here that is not having a good time.

pieces.title: Sunday Ride
pieces.subject: a cut-paper figure on a bicycle among stylised leaves and a yellow sun, blue and coral shapes scattered like wind
pieces.label: A blue cyclist rides through a flurry of cut leaves, coral scarf flying, under a yellow sun with spiky rays. The wheels are two perfect blue circles, the kind you only get with scissors after years of practice. Matisse said he wanted his art to be something like a good armchair for a tired man. This is the armchair, on a Sunday, going downhill.

artists.name: Piet Mondrian
artists.wallText: Mondrian reduced the world to black lines and three colours and then, in his last years in New York, let the lines dance. His last paintings were maps of a city that moved. Our cities move on a screen now.
artists.styleBrief: De Stijl neoplastic oil painting, a grid of black horizontal and vertical lines of varying thickness on white, rectangles filled with pure red, yellow and blue, some lines broken into small stuttering blocks of colour like lights along a route, strict flatness, hand-painted edges slightly imperfect, matte surface
artists.subjectRule: Modern grids and routes: transit maps, spreadsheets, app icons, circuit boards.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, flat even lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Metro Boogie Woogie
pieces.subject: a grid of black and coloured lines in which the lines are made of small alternating red, yellow, blue and grey blocks like stations on a transit map, a few larger coloured rectangles
pieces.label: Black lines divide the white canvas into rooms, and along some of them run chains of small red, yellow, blue and grey squares, the stops on a line. Here and there a big block of colour sits like a district. Mondrian arrived in New York in 1940, fell for the grid of Manhattan and put its traffic into *Broadway Boogie Woogie*. This is the same city, seen from underneath.

pieces.title: Composition with Cells
pieces.subject: a dense fine grid of thin black lines with many small white rectangles and a few cells filled solid yellow, red and blue, one cell outlined thicker
pieces.label: A fine black grid breaks the canvas into dozens of small white cells, and a few of them are filled: yellow, red, blue. One cell, right of centre, is outlined in a heavier black line, the one somebody clicked. Mondrian would spend weeks moving a line by a few millimetres. He would have understood the rest of us, formatting cells at half past five.

pieces.title: Composition: Home Screen
pieces.subject: a vertical grid of equal-sized rectangles, most white, a few in red, yellow and blue, a single wide blue rectangle across the bottom
pieces.label: A vertical grid of rectangles, most of them white, a few red, yellow or blue, and along the bottom one wide blue band that holds everything up. It is a phone's home screen, and it is also very nearly a Mondrian from the early twenties. He wanted a picture with nothing in it you could name. We turned it into the thing we look at most, and named every square.

pieces.title: Composition: Board
pieces.subject: a grid of black lines with small square nodes at intersections, thin yellow traces branching, one large red rectangle
pieces.label: Black lines, small square nodes where they cross, and thin yellow traces climbing a ladder up the left-hand side. A big red rectangle fills most of the right, as quiet as a chip. Mondrian believed the right lines in the right proportions could show the order underneath everything. He meant the universe. He did not expect it to run at three gigahertz.

pieces.title: Traffic Boogie Woogie
pieces.subject: two thick black lines crossing at the centre, made of stuttering red and yellow blocks, small blue squares clustered at the crossing
pieces.label: Two thick lines cross in the middle of the canvas, and neither is black: they are made of stuttering red and yellow blocks, like cars bunched at a light. Where they meet, small blue squares gather. In New York, Mondrian swapped his black lines for lines of colour, because the city had set everything in motion. At this crossing it has stopped moving again.

artists.name: Pablo Picasso
artists.wallText: Cubism was a way of telling the truth about looking: you never see a face from one angle, you assemble it from many. A world seen through front cameras, rear cameras and mirrors is already cubist. Someone just has to paint it.
artists.styleBrief: Analytical and synthetic Cubist oil painting, a figure or object fractured into overlapping geometric planes seen from several angles at once, muted ochres, greys and slate blues with passages of bold flat colour, heavy black contour lines, both eyes on one side of a face, collage-like flatness, chalky matte surface
artists.subjectRule: People with their devices, seen from every angle at once.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, flat even lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Woman Taking a Selfie
pieces.subject: a woman holding a phone at arm's length, her face shown simultaneously in profile, frontal view and reflected in the phone screen, fractured planes of ochre and grey
pieces.label: She holds her phone at arm's length, and her face is in three places at once: in profile at the left, straight on in the middle, and small on the screen in her hand. Planes of ochre, grey and slate lock them together. Picasso broke faces apart to show every side at once. The front camera does that for anyone who has ever gone looking for their good side.

pieces.title: The Meeting, Nine Tiles
pieces.subject: a grid of nine fragmented faces on a laptop screen, each face broken into planes, one with a hand raised, one muted
pieces.label: Nine faces in nine tiles on a laptop screen, each broken into planes and looking in a slightly different direction. One has raised a hand. One has a grey bar across the mouth. Nobody is looking at anybody. Cubism showed one sitter from many viewpoints at once. The video meeting shows many sitters from one viewpoint, all of them hoping someone else will speak.

pieces.title: Man with Earbuds
pieces.subject: a man in a cap listening with white earbuds, head tilted, his skull, ear and jaw shown as overlapping angular planes in grey and blue
pieces.label: A man in a cap tilts his head, a white earbud in the ear nearest us, its cable dropping down his chest. His face is a stack of grey and blue planes, and the ear is drawn twice, once as an ear and once as a shape. Picasso painted guitarists until the man and the guitar were one instrument. The guitar has gone. He is still listening to something.

pieces.title: Rider on an Electric Scooter
pieces.subject: a figure on an electric scooter fractured into motion, several wheels and handlebars at once, a helmet, bold flat red and black
pieces.label: A rider in a red helmet stands on an electric scooter that has too many handlebars and too many wheels, because it is moving and Picasso shows every position at once. The palette is ochre and grey, with the red and black of the scooter snapping through it. The Futurists painted speed, and Picasso thought they were showing off. Here, for once, he shows off.

pieces.title: Cat on the Keyboard
pieces.subject: a cat sprawled across a laptop keyboard, its body a set of curved and angular planes, the screen tilted at an impossible angle
pieces.label: A cat lies across a laptop keyboard, its body a set of curved and angular planes, one paw on the keys and one eye on us. The screen tips back at an angle no hinge allows. Picasso painted cats catching birds as scenes of plain cruelty. This cat is doing something crueller. It has sat on the one thing you need, and it knows.

artists.name: Edward Hopper
artists.wallText: Hopper painted a country that had just learned to stay up all night and did not yet know what to do with the time. Diners, gas stations, hotel rooms, offices at dusk. Every one of those places is still open. Only the light source has changed.
artists.styleBrief: American realist oil painting of the 1940s, hard clear light casting long precise shadows, simplified architectural geometry with strong horizontals, a muted but saturated palette of ochre, brick red, viridian and pale cream, a single still figure isolated in a public space, psychological quiet, cinematic framing from slightly outside the scene, smooth restrained brushwork
artists.subjectRule: The loneliness of the always-on city. Screens and fluorescent tubes are the new shop-window light.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting, even gallery lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Night Shift
pieces.subject: a woman alone in a 24-hour laundromat at three in the morning seen through the plate glass window from the empty street, fluorescent light spilling onto the pavement, rows of machines, a folded newspaper
pieces.label: We stand on the dark pavement and look in through the plate glass, where one woman waits at a row of washing machines under fluorescent tubes at three in the morning. The light from inside lies on the paving at our feet. Hopper painted *Nighthawks* from the same spot, outside the window, as if we were only passing. The machines are the only ones talking.

pieces.title: Charging
pieces.subject: a man sitting in a parked electric car at a charging station at dusk, lit by the dashboard glow, a flat suburban strip mall and an empty parking lot behind, last orange light on the horizon
pieces.label: A man sits in a pale car beside a charging post as the last orange light goes down behind a strip mall, and the car park stretches empty around him. The lamp is not on yet. He is not going anywhere for forty minutes. Hopper's *Gas* is a petrol station at dusk, the attendant alone with his pumps. The pump has become a plug. The wait has got longer.

pieces.title: Co-Working, Sunday
pieces.subject: a nearly empty glass-walled co-working space, one woman at a long table beside the window, morning sun in a hard diagonal across the floor, a plant, closed laptops
pieces.label: Sunday morning in a glass office, and the sun lays a hard diagonal across the orange wall and the floor. One woman works at a long table by the window, back straight, laptop open, while every other chair is empty. A plant keeps her company. Hopper loved rooms like this, where the light arrives with more purpose than the people. She came in to get ahead. The sun got here first.

pieces.title: Departures, 6 a.m.
pieces.subject: an airport gate with rows of empty seats, one traveler standing at the window looking out at the tarmac, pale early light, a grounded plane
pieces.label: A traveller in a dark suit stands at the window with his hands behind his back, looking out at a grounded plane with a red tail. Rows of empty seats throw long shadows across the polished floor. It is six in the morning and nobody else has come. Hopper's people stand at windows waiting for something he never paints. This one has a boarding pass. It does not seem to help.

pieces.title: Delivery
pieces.subject: a food delivery rider resting on his bicycle under a single streetlight outside a closed diner at night, the glow of his phone on his face, a dark street with one lit window
pieces.label: A delivery rider rests on his bicycle under a single streetlamp beside a shuttered shop with a striped awning, and the only other light is his phone, glowing on his face. The street runs off into the dark, where one far lamp answers his. Hopper painted the night city as a string of lit islands. The rider lives between them, waiting for the next order to send him on.

artists.name: Mark Rothko
artists.wallText: Rothko wanted people to cry in front of his paintings, and they did. Soft-edged rectangles of colour that seem to breathe. He was painting light before there were screens that glow. Every glowing rectangle since owes him.
artists.styleBrief: Colour field abstract oil painting, two or three large soft-edged rectangles of colour floating on a coloured ground, edges feathered and bleeding, thin translucent layers glowing from within, monumental scale, no line, no figure, quiet emotional intensity, matte velvety surface with subtle brush drag
artists.subjectRule: The colours of modern light: screens, LEDs, sunsets through pollution, neon in fog. Each piece is one specific glow.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the large oil painting, dim even gallery lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Untitled (Standby)
pieces.subject: a large soft-edged deep black rectangle above a thin glowing red rectangle on a charcoal ground
pieces.label: A great black rectangle hangs above a thin band of red, both floating on a charcoal ground. Stand close, as Rothko asked people to, and the black turns out to be several blacks, and the red glows faintly from underneath. It is the colour of a television in a dark room, off but not quite. Rothko's dark late paintings were a kind of vigil. So is standby.

pieces.title: Untitled (Night Mode)
pieces.subject: two soft rectangles of warm amber and dull orange stacked on a dark brown ground, glowing faintly
pieces.label: Two soft rectangles, amber above and orange below, glow on a dark brown ground like a lamp behind a curtain. The edges breathe. Rothko wanted colour to do the work of a feeling, with no picture in the way. Night mode does exactly this to a screen: it takes the blue out and leaves you something warm to fall asleep in front of.

pieces.title: Untitled (Sunset, Air Quality Poor)
pieces.subject: a hazy pink-orange rectangle over a murky violet-grey rectangle on a dusty tan ground
pieces.label: A hazy pink-orange rectangle floats above a murky violet-grey one, on a ground the colour of dust. It is beautiful, and it is beautiful for a bad reason. Rothko's glowing colours were meant to hold something eternal. These are the colours you get over a motorway in August, when the air is poor, and they move people just as much. That is the uncomfortable part.

pieces.title: Untitled (Blue Light)
pieces.subject: a cold pale blue rectangle floating on a deep navy ground with a thin band of white light at the horizon between them
pieces.label: A cold pale-blue rectangle hangs above a deep navy one, and between them, like a horizon, runs a thin line of white light. The whole painting glows the way a phone does in a dark bedroom. Rothko made his chapel in Houston nearly black, so that the light would have to come from inside the paintings. This light comes from inside too, at three a.m., with a buzz.

pieces.title: Untitled (Loading)
pieces.subject: three soft grey rectangles of slightly different greys on a pale grey ground, almost invisible edges
pieces.label: Three soft grey rectangles on a pale grey ground, the middle one nudged a little to the right, their edges so faint they are nearly not there. Nothing has arrived yet. Rothko said silence was so accurate, and he meant it as praise. This is the most accurate painting in the room: the three bars of a page that has not loaded, held for ever in the moment before.

artists.name: Frida Kahlo
artists.wallText: Kahlo painted herself because, she said, she was the subject she knew best. Her self-portraits are direct, botanical, unsentimental about pain. The self-portrait is now the most common image on earth. She would have had opinions.
artists.styleBrief: Mid-century Mexican folk-modernist oil painting, a frontal figure with an unflinching direct gaze against dense tropical foliage, flat saturated greens, reds and golds, small symbolic animals and objects, naive precise detail, a votive ex-voto stillness, matte paint on board
artists.subjectRule: Modern bodies, modern medicine, modern selfhood. Frontal, symbolic, unsentimental.
artists.renderSuffix: museum photograph of the oil painting on board, flat even lighting, no frame, no text, no wall, no floor, cropped to the canvas edge

pieces.title: Self-Portrait with Insulin Pump
pieces.subject: a frontal self-portrait of a young woman with short cropped grey-streaked hair and thin brows, an invented person who resembles no real painter, an insulin pump visible at her waist, surrounded by dense green leaves and a hummingbird
pieces.label: She faces us square on, grey-streaked hair cropped short, in an embroidered blouse, and at her waist, clipped to her skirt, is an insulin pump with its little screen lit. Around her the jungle is crowded: a monkey, a hummingbird, a deer, a tortoise, a heart in flames. Kahlo painted her medical history as calmly as her flowers. The pump belongs in this company. It keeps her alive too.

pieces.title: The Two Fridas, Front Camera
pieces.subject: two seated versions of the same woman with a shaved head and round glasses, an invented person who resembles no real painter, holding hands, one seen directly and one as she appears on a phone screen, connected by a thin red charging cable
pieces.label: Two seated women with shaved heads and round glasses, identical, barefoot, in the same white blouse and red skirt. The one on the right is the same woman on a phone screen, and a red charging cable runs from one to the other where Kahlo's *Two Fridas* share an artery. Parrots and a monkey watch from the leaves. It is a portrait of a person and her profile.

pieces.title: Self-Portrait with Rescue Dog
pieces.subject: a frontal portrait of a woman with long loose red hair and flowers tucked behind one ear, an invented person who resembles no real painter, a small scruffy terrier sitting on the table beside her, a bougainvillea wall behind
pieces.label: A woman with long loose red hair and a white flower behind one ear sits at a table with her hands folded, looking straight at us. Beside her, on the table, a small scruffy terrier looks straight at us too. Bougainvillea fills the wall behind. Kahlo painted herself with her monkeys, parrots and hairless dogs as family. The rescue dog is family. You can tell because he is on the table.

pieces.title: The Scan
pieces.subject: a woman with a blonde bob standing frontally in a hospital gown, an invented person who resembles no real painter, holding an MRI scan of her own spine like a votive image, leaves and small flames around her
